title: Inclusive education with AI: supporting special needs and tackling language barriers
extended_summary:
This paper reviews how artificial intelligence can support inclusive education, with a focus on two major barriers in K-12 settings: language differences and special educational needs. It asks how AI tools are being used in classrooms, what benefits they may provide, what limitations they have, and what implementation conditions are needed to use them responsibly and effectively.

The paper synthesizes recent literature, case studies, white papers, and policy reports from education, accessibility, and AI research. It discusses AI translation and captioning tools for multilingual classrooms, generative AI for bilingual materials, and assistive technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, adaptive learning platforms, VR/AR, robots, emotion-recognition tools, diagnostic systems, and accessibility features. The review frames these tools as supports for students with disabilities, multilingual learners, teachers, parents, and schools, primarily in K-12 contexts, though it does not report a single primary sample or intervention study.

The main conclusion is that AI can improve comprehension, engagement, access, and personalization, but only when used as a complement to teacher-led instruction and human oversight. The paper emphasizes that effectiveness depends on infrastructure, equitable access, cultural and linguistic accuracy, privacy protections, and thoughtful pedagogical use. It recommends gradual reduction of AI dependence over time, hybrid instructional approaches, and ethical implementation frameworks so that AI supports inclusion without widening existing inequities.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A general category of generative AI tools and AI-enabled educational applications, including chatbots, translation apps, captioning/subtitling tools, adaptive learning systems, assistive technologies, and diagnostic platforms used to support inclusive K-12 education.
identified_tools.use_case: This is a review paper examining how generative AI and related AI tools are integrated into K-12 inclusive education, especially literacy/language support and special needs instruction. It discusses examples such as ChatGPT, DeepL, Google Translate, Duolingo, Otter.ai, Rev.com, and other AI-driven systems, but does not empirically evaluate a single named product as the study focus.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that AI-driven translation, captioning, bilingual content generation, and tutoring tools can improve comprehension, participation, engagement, and perceived inclusion for multilingual learners and students with disabilities. It also notes that benefits are contingent on careful implementation, human oversight, and equitable access; no pooled effect size is reported for the review itself.
findings.measure: Reported outcomes across included studies and case examples, including comprehension, participation, engagement, and inclusion

findings.finding_summary: The paper states that AI translation and bilingual content tools can support literacy-related skills by helping learners understand vocabulary, follow lessons, and perform closer to native-speaking peers in comprehension assessments. It also describes AI tools for reading support, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and adaptive literacy learning as promising for students with reading difficulties and language barriers.
findings.measure: Reading comprehension, vocabulary support, and literacy engagement across cited studies

findings.finding_summary: The review synthesizes evidence that AI language tools and chatbots can provide immediate feedback, simulated practice, and personalized pathways that support language learning and proficiency development. At the same time, it warns that overreliance may impede independent language skill development, so AI should complement rather than replace direct communication and traditional instruction.
findings.measure: Language proficiency, participation in language practice, and learner autonomy across cited studies

findings.finding_summary: Across special education applications, the review reports that AI-based assistive technologies, adaptive learning systems, interactive robots, VR/AR, and early diagnostic tools can improve accessibility, independence, engagement, and individualized support. The paper emphasizes that these gains depend on implementation conditions such as teacher training, infrastructure, data privacy protections, and context-sensitive use.
findings.measure: Accessibility, independence, engagement, individualized support, and diagnostic utility across cited studies

quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/integrated review with examples drawn from many prior studies rather than a single empirical evaluation of one tool. The paper does not report a new controlled design or pooled quantitative estimate for the tools it discusses.
impact_tier_rationale: The review describes potentially meaningful benefits for literacy, language support, and inclusion, but the evidence is synthesized from heterogeneous sources and many outcomes are qualitative or non-quantified. Because no single effect size is reported, the magnitude of impact is unclear at the paper level.
